title: How to work cross-stitch on dark fabric
subtitle: Adapting needle and light technique for black, navy, and dark Aida
excerpt: Cross-stitching on dark fabric needs good light, a slightly larger needle, and a lighter floss count than pale Aida. The holes are harder to see and the thread does not show the stitches as the chart suggests unless the coverage is checked as you go.
sourceNotes: Established practice for dark-ground cross-stitch documented in needlework periodicals from the 1880s onward. The Weldon's Practical Needlework series (1880s, Internet Archive) includes guidance on working on coloured and dark grounds.

content.text: is the same motion as stitching on pale Aida, but the holes are harder to locate by eye and pale thread on a dark ground reads differently from dark thread on pale ground. Good light and a consistent hold on the fabric are the two adjustments that make the biggest difference.

Dark Aida is most commonly black, navy, or charcoal. The weave is identical to pale Aida; the grid of holes is the same size. The visual difference is that there is no contrast between the thread and the fabric to guide the eye to the holes. The technique is to feel for the holes with the needle tip and trust the count rather than looking for the contrast the pale fabric gives.
Use a daylight lamp or LED lamp positioned directly over the work, not behind you. The light must shine through the Aida grid to make the holes visible.
Try a slightly larger needle than usual for the fabric count, such as a size 22
on 14-count rather than the standard size 24. The thicker shaft makes it easier to feel the hole before committing the thread.
Mount the fabric in the hoop with a white or pale cloth behind it. The pale backing makes the holes visible from the front by creating contrast through the Aida grid.
Use at least three strands of

on 14-count dark fabric for solid coverage. Two strands looks thin on dark backgrounds because the dark ground shows through the gaps between threads. Three strands gives even coverage; the stitches should lie smooth against the dark ground, not show gaps at the centre of each cross.
Grid the fabric before starting with a 10-by-10 basting grid. The grid lets you count by squares rather than by visual contrast.

items.symptom: The thread coverage looks thin and the dark ground shows through
items.cause: Too few strands, or the strands were not lying parallel to each other in the finished cross.
items.fix: Add a strand (go from two to three). Check that the strands lie parallel rather than twisted inside the stitch; separated strands give better coverage.

items.symptom: The needle keeps going into the wrong hole
items.cause: Stitching in poor light or without a backing cloth to show the holes.
items.fix: Use a daylight lamp pointed directly at the work. Hold the hoop up to the light at a slight angle if needed to see the holes more clearly.

content.text: Dark Aida suits designs with pale or bright colours where the contrast with the background is part of the effect. A quotes-and-sayings piece in white thread on black Aida reads cleanly and works well as a framed piece.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.
A blunt-tipped needle that slips between fabric threads instead of piercing them. Size 24 is the default for 14ct Aida; finer fabrics need a higher-number, finer needle.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.
